items.label: f04-utc-today
items.front: At 9pm in New York (already the next day in UTC) a user picks tomorrow's date as a due date. normalizeDueDate rejects `value <= toDateOnly(new Date())`, where toDateOnly uses the UTC calendar. Evidence: taskService.js:177-179. What does the user see?
items.back: 'Due date must be in the future.' for a date that is tomorrow from their point of view, because 'today' is computed in UTC, not the user's calendar. Fix: decide whose calendar defines 'today' (send the client's date or timezone) and test the rule at a day boundary.

items.label: f03-last-write-wins
items.front: Two tabs edit the same task from the same loaded copy. The model updates with `where({ id })` and the tasks table has no version column. Evidence: taskModel.js:71-81. What does the second save do?
items.back: It succeeds and overwrites the first save without anyone noticing (lost update). Fix: add a `version` column, update `WHERE id = ? AND version = ?`, increment it, and return 409 when zero rows match so the client can reload and retry.

items.label: f02-sanitize-destroys-text
items.front: A user saves the title `Fix a < b check in sort`. sanitizeString runs `.replace(/[<>]/g, '')` on every title and description before storage. Evidence: sanitize.js:7-9. What is the consequence?
items.back: The stored title is silently changed to `Fix a  b check in sort` — normalization that destroys user data, not validation. Fix: store the text as typed and escape on output (React already escapes), or reject the characters with a 400 if they are truly disallowed.

items.label: f01-pg-date-timezone
items.front: The server runs in a timezone east of UTC (e.g. Europe/Berlin). due_date is a Postgres `date`, node-postgres hands it back as a JS Date at LOCAL midnight, and the unchanged-date check formats it with `toISOString().slice(0, 10)`. Evidence: taskService.js:276-277, toDateOnly at :27-29. What goes wrong?
items.back: Local midnight is the previous day in UTC, so the stored 2020-01-01 formats as 2019-12-31, the 'unchanged' date no longer matches, and an overdue task becomes uneditable again. Fix: keep `date` columns as strings (pg setTypeParser for OID 1082) or format with local getters, and run the overdue test under a UTC+ TZ.

items.prompt: `2099-02-30` matches the `^\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}$` pattern. What actually rejects it in normalizeDueDate?

choices.text: new Date('2099-02-30T00:00:00.000Z') is an Invalid Date, so the NaN check fires
It rolls over to March 2, so formatting it back no longer equals the input
Postgres rejects the date on insert, and that error is mapped to a 400
The future-date comparison fails, because the string sorts before today

choices: new Date('2099-02-30T00:00:00.000Z') is an Invalid Date, so the NaN check fires
It rolls over to March 2, so formatting it back no longer equals the input
Postgres rejects the date on insert, and that error is mapped to a 400
The future-date comparison fails, because the string sorts before today

items.explanation: JavaScript Date normalizes overflowing days; the round-trip `toDateOnly(parsed) !== value` is what detects an impossible calendar date.

items.prompt: For Exercise 1 a learner writes `query.whereRaw("title ILIKE '%" + q + "%'")`. Besides injection, why does the review demand a test whose search term contains `%` and `'`?

choices.text: Express decodes a percent sign in the URL twice, which the test detects
Postgres ILIKE is unable to compare strings that contain a percent sign
sanitizeString strips the quote character, so the test checks sanitizing
They break or widen a concatenated pattern; the test proves the term is bound

choices: Express decodes a percent sign in the URL twice, which the test detects
Postgres ILIKE is unable to compare strings that contain a percent sign
sanitizeString strips the quote character, so the test checks sanitizing
They break or widen a concatenated pattern; the test proves the term is bound

items.explanation: A quote ends the SQL literal (error or injection) and `%` acts as a wildcard; binding via whereILike plus an exact-match assertion proves the term is bound and matches only the intended rows.

items.prompt: Two users open the same task, each changes the priority and saves a few seconds apart. With the current updateTask, what happens?

choices.text: Postgres merges both changes, since they arrive in two separate statements
Both get 200, and the second silently overwrites the first (UPDATE by id only)
The second PUT blocks until the first transaction commits, and then it fails
The second PUT gets 409, because updated_at changed since that user loaded it

choices: Postgres merges both changes, since they arrive in two separate statements
Both get 200, and the second silently overwrites the first (UPDATE by id only)
The second PUT blocks until the first transaction commits, and then it fails
The second PUT gets 409, because updated_at changed since that user loaded it

items.explanation: The UPDATE matches on id alone and there is no version column; `where({ id }).update(...)` is last-write-wins. Exercise 3's fix updates `WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` and answers 409 on zero rows.

items.prompt: A task stored with due_date 2020-01-01 is edited twice: first `{ title, due_date: '2020-01-01' }`, then `{ due_date: '2020-01-02' }`. Which outcome does the service produce, and why?

choices.text: First 200, then 400: only a date equal to the stored one skips the future-date rule
Both 400: each submitted due_date has to be in the future, overdue task or not
Both 200: once a task is overdue, the future-date rule is switched off for it
First 400, then 200: the title edit is what gets blocked while a task is overdue

choices: First 200, then 400: only a date equal to the stored one skips the future-date rule
Both 400: each submitted due_date has to be in the future, overdue task or not
Both 200: once a task is overdue, the future-date rule is switched off for it
First 400, then 200: the title edit is what gets blocked while a task is overdue

items.explanation: A submitted date equal to the stored one bypasses the future-date rule, but any changed date is validated again. Line 277 compares the payload with the stored date normalized to YYYY-MM-DD and only calls normalizeDueDate when they differ; the exception is deliberately narrow.

items.prompt: getTaskStats wraps each grouped row with `Number(row.count)`. If someone removes that conversion, what does `stats.total` become with counts 2 and 3?

choices.text: 5, because the driver already converts COUNT results to numbers
NaN, because adding a string to a number produces NaN in JavaScript
The string "023": COUNT comes back as text, so += concatenates
A thrown TypeError, because bigint and number values do not mix

choices: 5, because the driver already converts COUNT results to numbers
NaN, because adding a string to a number produces NaN in JavaScript
The string "023": COUNT comes back as text, so += concatenates
A thrown TypeError, because bigint and number values do not mix

items.explanation: Postgres COUNT is a bigint, and node-postgres returns int8 as strings to avoid precision loss; `0 + '2'` is '02', then '02' + '3' is '023'.

items.prompt: The title column is already `varchar(255)`, so Postgres would refuse a 256-character title anyway. What would the client see if the service did NOT check the length first?

choices.text: A 400 VALIDATION_ERROR, because the middleware maps database errors to client errors
A 201, because Postgres silently truncates an over-long title to 255 characters
A 500 INTERNAL_ERROR, since a raw database error is not an operational AppError
A 409 conflict, because the middleware reports constraint violations as conflicts

A 201, because Postgres silently truncates an over-long title to 255 characters
A 500 INTERNAL_ERROR, since a raw database error is not an operational AppError
A 409 conflict, because the middleware reports constraint violations as conflicts

items.explanation: errorHandler only passes through `AppError` with isOperational; anything else becomes status 500 'An unexpected error occurred.'. Validating first turns expected bad input into a useful 400.

items.prompt: taskModel.listTasks interpolates `filters.order` straight into `orderByRaw`. What keeps `?order=asc;DROP TABLE tasks` from reaching SQL?

choices.text: The service allowlists order to asc/desc and throws a 400 before the model runs
Knex escapes each orderByRaw string, so the interpolation is bound like a parameter
Express rejects query strings that contain semicolons before the route matches
Postgres refuses multiple statements in one query, so the payload is harmless

Knex escapes each orderByRaw string, so the interpolation is bound like a parameter
Express rejects query strings that contain semicolons before the route matches
Postgres refuses multiple statements in one query, so the payload is harmless

items.explanation: normalizeListFilters calls validateAllowedValue('order', ..., ['asc','desc']); the model trusts only already-validated filters, so the raw fragment is safe only because of that layer.

items.prompt: The test requests `GET /api/tasks/9007199254740992` and expects 400. Why would checking the id with Number.isInteger alone let this request through?

choices.text: Number.isInteger returns false for strings, so the id would be rejected before parsing
Number.isInteger already rejects values above 2147483647, the Postgres integer limit
Number('9007199254740992') is NaN, which Number.isInteger already treats as invalid
2^53 is an integer but not a safe one: isInteger accepts it, isSafeInteger does not

Number('9007199254740992') is NaN, which Number.isInteger already treats as invalid

items.explanation: 2^53 cannot be told apart from its neighbouring values. parseTaskId uses `Number.isSafeInteger(id)` plus the 1..2147483647 range; the guide notes that Number.isInteger alone is insufficient.

choices.text: 201 with the title stored as '<>', because sanitizing just trims whitespace
400 'Title is required and must be a string.', since brackets are not text
201 with an empty title, because the length check runs before sanitizing
400 'Title is required.': brackets are stripped, then the empty check runs

items.prompt: A client sends `PUT /api/tasks/7` with body `{ "status": "done" }` and no title. Why does the stored title survive instead of failing title validation or being blanked?

choices.text: buildUpdatePayload only touches keys the body owns, so title never enters the update
normalizeTitle falls back to the existing row's title when the incoming one is undefined
The controller merges the request body over the stored row before calling the service
Knex drops undefined values from the update, so validation runs but the column is skipped

choices: buildUpdatePayload only touches keys the body owns, so title never enters the update
normalizeTitle falls back to the existing row's title when the incoming one is undefined
The controller merges the request body over the stored row before calling the service
Knex drops undefined values from the update, so validation runs but the column is skipped

items.explanation: buildUpdatePayload only normalizes fields the body actually owns: `hasOwn(payload, 'title')` is false for an omitted key, so `updates.title` is never assigned; a supplied `null` would be present and would be validated.

items.prompt: The 'invalid inputs' test asserts each POST returns 400 AND compares the row count before and after. What would the status check alone fail to catch?

choices.text: A handler that returns 422 instead of 400 for the same bad input
A handler that writes the row and then throws, still answering 400
A slow handler that runs past the default node:test timeout
A validation message whose wording changed between two releases

choices: A handler that returns 422 instead of 400 for the same bad input
A handler that writes the row and then throws, still answering 400
A slow handler that runs past the default node:test timeout
A validation message whose wording changed between two releases

items.explanation: Such a handler still answers 400 but leaves a persisted record behind. The invariant is 'invalid input never creates rows'; only reading authoritative state (the table count) observes it - a response code is not evidence about persistence.

It is left out of the update, because the status value did not change
It becomes null, because completed_at is set by the toggle endpoint alone
It keeps last week's timestamp, since the stored completion time is reused
